1.title: Pinot Blanc (Klevner / Weissclevner) and Auxerrois
1.html:
Pinot Blanc is the white mutation of the Pinot family (Pinot Noir / Pinot Gris), generally thought to originate in Burgundy, and was first documented only in the 17th century. Yields are generous (50–70 hl/ha), natural alcohol can reach 9.8°–13.8°, and it is often used as a base for Crémant and is frequently blended or labelled together with Auxerrois.

Auxerrois is often counted together with Pinot Blanc in statistics (the planted areas overlap heavily): its acidity is slightly lower and its alcohol slightly higher, so the wine is usually rounder and easier to drink, but may be a little less refined than Pinot Blanc itself.

Style: often better than Sylvaner, dry and smooth with pleasant supporting acidity — an everyday wine you "don't have to think about, just enjoy"; suited to cold dishes (pork / duck / rabbit terrine, ham and asparagus rolls) and hot dishes (ham in puff pastry, creamed stews, sweetbreads in pastry, poultry stews). It covers 21.21% of plantings, almost level with Riesling for first place.
2.title: Sylvaner: A Friendly Everyday Choice
2.html:
Introduced in the late 18th century, thought to come from Austria or Transylvania, and especially popular in Bas-Rhin. High yields (100–200 hl/ha), with relatively weak vine vigour.

Style: fresh and fruity, light or somewhat weightier depending on origin; essentially an approachable, easy "all-purpose wine", and from a good terroir it can reach a delicacy close to Riesling (though without Riesling's lively acid tension) — an excellent "bar wine" (vin de comptoir).

Classic pairings: onion tart, seafood, fried fish, sauerkraut, small appetisers, marinated herring, ham and sausage platters, lightly cured salmon. It covers 11% of plantings.
3.title: Pinot Noir: The Only Red Grape Variety
3.html:
Pinot Noir was probably the earliest variety brought to Alsace from Burgundy (Bourgogne) (the two regions are geographically close), held an important place in the Middle Ages, then declined and survived only in a few villages (Ottrott, Marlenheim, Rodern). It was traditionally made into rosé, but recently there has been a trend of "returning to red".

An early-ripening variety with small, compact bunches and small, slightly oval, black-purple berries. It grows best on limestone slopes with slightly clayey loam, and mid-slope often gives the best balance between body and delicacy.

Style: both rosé and red have pleasant fruit and are popular with consumers; reds from excellent vintages can be quite impressive. Rosé is soft and easy to drink, occasionally slightly spritzy (perlant), and suited to being served chilled. Pairings: roast poultry, pan-fried game, braised beef shoulder with Pinot Noir; the rosé goes with country pâté, ham and sausage, lentil and bacon salad, roast saddle of rabbit, and even grilled fish. It covers 9% of plantings.
4.title: Other Varieties: Chasselas and Chardonnay
4.html:
• Chasselas (Gutedel): introduced in the late 18th century; fresh, neutral flavour, suited to young early drinking. Its plantings keep shrinking (only about 1%), it is now rarely seen on the market, and is mainly used in Edelzwicker blends.
  • Chardonnay: allowed only in Crémant d'Alsace and not in ordinary still Alsace wine; it adds delicacy, freshness and extended ageing potential to Crémant.
  • Banned varieties: Knipperlé, Goldriesling, Müller-Thurgau and Meunier have no longer been permitted in Alsace wine since 1980.
5.question: Pinot Noir is Alsace's only red grape variety. What was it traditionally mainly made into?
5.options.1: Rosé — good red only in a very few excellent vintages
5.explanation: Pinot Noir is the only black grape variety grown in Alsace and was traditionally made mostly into rosé — Alsace's cool climate makes it hard for black grapes to reach the ripeness needed for quality red wine, so only in a very few exceptional vintages can truly good red be produced, although a "return to red" trend has emerged in recent years.
6.message: Variety lessons complete! You now have the core spectrum of Alsace varieties.
6.keyPoints.0: Pinot Blanc (21.21%) and Auxerrois overlap heavily in statistics; an easy everyday wine and a common Crémant base
6.keyPoints.1: Sylvaner (11%) is approachable and, from good terroir, can approach the delicacy of Riesling — an excellent bar wine
6.keyPoints.2: Pinot Noir (9%) is the only black grape variety, traditionally made into rosé, with a recent trend of returning to red
6.keyPoints.3: Chasselas plantings keep shrinking and it is mainly used in Edelzwicker; Chardonnay is allowed only in Crémant
